title: Content maturity, drawn
subject: A maturity model of content development: four levels from Markdown notes to a view built into the app

brief.background: Content in the owner's repos starts as Markdown notes and sometimes becomes rows of data, a page, and a view inside an app. The owner named this a maturity model of content development, with Markdown as the first level. One SVG diagram should let a reader say: content matures through four levels, notes, data, page and app; each step up costs upkeep and is taken only when the content's use calls for it; and a page built on notes is still level 1. It should also let a reader place a piece of content on a level and name its next move, or decide it should not move.
brief.methodology: Eight concepts were sketched before any was judged, each with a different explanatory mechanism, structure or borrowed form. Each had to show the four levels, what moves content up a level and when that is worth doing, and where at least one real example sits. The Capability Maturity Model, bronze-silver-gold data tiers and Technology Readiness Levels were the analogies brought to it.

ideas.title: Staircase
ideas.commentary:
The form maturity models are usually drawn in: four steps rising left to right, each a level, each riser labeled with the move that climbs it. Height reads as maturity at a glance, and examples can stand on their step.

Its weakness is the one the brief warns about: a staircase implies that higher is better, while the model says to climb only as far as the use requires.

ideas.title: Layer stack
ideas.commentary:
Levels as layers, each resting on the one below. The point it makes best is dependency: a page needs data under it, so a page built straight on notes shows as a **gap**, which is exactly the Landscape.

It says less about the move between layers or when to make it.

ideas.title: Refinery
ideas.commentary:
Content flows left to right through four stations, from raw to refined, with a valve between stations that opens when the use calls for it. It borrows from the bronze, silver and gold data tiers.

The flow reads naturally, but it suggests everything should pass through, and it hides that content can move back.

ideas.title: Readiness checklist
ideas.commentary:
A vertical scale with one entry test per level, borrowed from Technology Readiness Levels: **you are at level 2 when the facts are rows and a check runs**. Placing content becomes a judgment anyone can repeat.

It is the most useful for a session applying the model and the least visual.

ideas.title: Two-axis grid
ideas.commentary:
How the content is held against where it is shown, with healthy content on the diagonal and failures off it: a page over notes sits below the diagonal. This was the earlier Map tab's frame.

It is precise but takes explaining, which is why it did not read on a phone.

ideas.title: Rings around the app
ideas.commentary:
The app at the center and the levels as rings around it, after the owner's own phrase about how far a page sits from the center of the Web Tools app. Examples are dots on their ring.

It fits the Web Tools app's own ring vocabulary, but distance from the app is only part of maturity; data has no clear ring.

ideas.title: Value and upkeep
ideas.commentary:
A small chart: what a reader gains rises with each level, and so does upkeep, faster at the top. The right level for a piece of content is where the two lines say stop.

It makes the climb-only-as-far rule concrete, but the curves are illustrative, not measured.

ideas.title: States and moves
ideas.commentary:
Four states with arrows up, each labeled with when to move, and an arrow back down for content whose use faded, as the CORE throughline went back to Markdown.

It is the only concept that shows moving back as normal, but it loses the sense of rising maturity.

grafts: the gap: a page resting on notes with the data step drawn empty, labeled with the Landscape
one entry test per level, so placing content is a judgment anyone can repeat
a return arrow: content can move back down when its use fades
selection.rationale: The owner chose the words maturity model, and the staircase is the form a reader recognizes for one. The grafts answer its weaknesses: the entry tests make each level checkable, the gap shows the one failure the repos actually have, and the return arrow tempers the suggestion that higher is always better.
assumptions: Does the staircase still say higher is better, even with the return arrow?
Is a check part of level 2's entry test, or a level of its own?
Will one entry test per level let a session place content without the document?
Does the figure need to read at full detail on a phone?
